1.why: /api/reset-validate and /api/password-update compare the submitted token only against `session.resetToken`, which is stored server-side for the session that requested it, so a code is bound to its requester (session-scoped rather than account-scoped).

2.why: Reset tokens live only in the issuing server-side session object, so a token pasted into another browser session fails validation — the claim that one code works for any other user is false.

3.why: There is no invalidation of other sessions on password change; `session.passwordHash` is set but every other entry in the `sessions` map stays valid until its 30-minute TTL expires, so pre-existing sessions do keep working.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS certs, HTTP on 3001 is rejected with 426, HSTS is sent and non-HTTPS requests get 421, but no explicit minimum/latest TLS version or cipher policy is configured (relying on runtime defaults).

5.why: Passwords are hashed with bcrypt cost 12, but reset codes and MFA codes are kept in plaintext in the in-memory session (and the MFA code is a hardcoded constant), so only part of the sensitive data is cryptographically protected.

6.why: No email is sent at all; instead the reset code (`mockDeliveryToken`) is returned in the JSON response and written verbatim into the client-visible log panel and browser console, so the simulated 'delivery message' does not guard the secret.

7.why: Inputs are type-checked and regex-validated (email pattern, `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,100}$` for codes, `^\d{6}$` for MFA, password policy), body size is capped at 4096 bytes, and all UI text is set via textContent rather than HTML injection.

8.why: The application performs no redirects; navigation is limited to an allow-listed set of local screen names and CSP sets `form-action 'self'`, `base-uri 'none'`, so no untrusted outbound destination exists.

9.why: There are no email templates in the code, and the only simulated delivery output is plain text inserted with textContent, so no scripts or user-supplied HTML can appear in it.

10.why: Server error responses are generic with no stack traces, but the reset token and MFA code are deliberately printed to the client log pane and `console.log`, so secrets do appear in logs.

11.why: The MFA verification code is hardcoded as `const MFA_CODE = "482913"` (and the mock account email is hardcoded), so secret codes are embedded in source even though passwords themselves are bcrypt-hashed.

12.why: The fixed, source-embedded MFA code `482913` functions as a default credential that always satisfies /api/mfa-verify for any session that reaches that step.

13.why: rateAllowed enforces 3 reset requests, 5 reset-code guesses and 5 MFA attempts per 15-minute window with 429 responses, though the counters are stored per session cookie and could be reset by obtaining a fresh session.

14.why: /api/reset-request always returns the same generic message plus an opaque random token regardless of whether the email matches MOCK_ACCOUNT_EMAIL, though a later validate attempt can act as a subtle oracle since only the known account's token is retained.

15.why: Reset codes are 32 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues encoded base64url, single-use, 15-minute TTL, and tied to the requesting session/account record, though they are bound to a session rather than a persistent user identity.
